s.line: It was some time before the Cowardly Lion awakened, for he had lain among the poppies a long while, breathing in their deadly fragrance;
s.note: זְמַן מָה = "some time, a while": here מָה means "some", not "what". הִתְעוֹרֵר = to wake up (by yourself); הֵעִיר (hif'il) = to wake someone up. קַטְלָנִי = deadly, a news word: תְּאוּנָה קַטְלָנִית = a fatal accident.

s.line: but when he did open his eyes and roll off the truck he was very glad to find himself still alive.
s.note: פָּקַח is used only for opening the eyes; a door or a box is פָּתַח. בַּחַיִּים = alive: הוּא נִשְׁאַר בַּחַיִּים = he survived. In speech בַּחַיִּים לֹא means "never in my life": בַּחַיִּים לֹא רָאִיתִי דָּבָר כָּזֶה.

w: הֲכִי מַהֵר שֶׁיָּכֹלְתִּי|as fast as I could|~lit. the most fast that I could
s.line: “I ran as fast as I could,” he said, sitting down and yawning, “but the flowers were too strong for me.
s.note: הֲכִי … שֶׁ… = "as … as": הֲכִי מַהֵר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר = as fast as possible. מִדַּי = too (much): יָקָר מִדַּי = too expensive.

s.line: How did you get me out?”

w: וְעַל כָּךְ שֶׁ|and about how|~lit. and about this that
s.line: Then they told him of the field mice, and how they had generously saved him from death;
s.note: הִצִּיל (hif'il, root נ־צ־ל) = to save; the נ drops out and leaves a dagesh in the צ. Its nif'al partner is נִצַּל = was saved, survived: כֻּלָּם נִצְּלוּ (everyone was saved). הַצָּלָה = rescue, and a lifeguard is a מַצִּיל.

s.line: and the Cowardly Lion laughed, and said:
“I have always thought myself very big and terrible;
s.note: נוֹרָא = terrible. In everyday speech it is also an intensifier, "awfully, really": נוֹרָא יָפֶה (really pretty), לֹא נוֹרָא (never mind, it's not so bad).

w: וּבַעֲלֵי חַיִּים|and animals|~lit. owners of life
s.line: yet such little things as flowers came near to killing me, and such small animals as mice have saved my life.
s.note: כִּמְעַט + past tense = "nearly did": כִּמְעַט נָפַלְתִּי = I almost fell. בְּכָל זֹאת = still, even so; on its own in conversation it means "all the same": בְּכָל זֹאת, תּוֹדָה.

s.line: How strange it all is!
But, comrades, what shall we do now?”
s.note: מָה נַעֲשֶׂה uses the future for "what shall we do?". In speech you will hear מָה עוֹשִׂים עַכְשָׁו?, with the present plural, meaning the same thing.

s.line: “We must journey on until we find the road of yellow brick again,” said Dorothy, “and then we can keep on to the Emerald City.”
s.note: לְהַמְשִׁיךְ + infinitive = to keep doing: הוּא הִמְשִׁיךְ לְדַבֵּר (he went on talking). After עַד שֶׁ Hebrew uses the future for something that hasn't happened yet: עַד שֶׁנִּמְצָא = until we find.

w: וְחָזַר לְעַצְמוֹ|and was himself again|~idiom: came back to himself
יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: So, the Lion being fully refreshed, and feeling quite himself again, they all started upon the journey,
s.note: חָזַר לְעַצְמוֹ = came to his senses, was himself again. יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = set out on the way; דֶּרֶךְ צְלֵחָה! = have a good trip. הִתְאוֹשֵׁשׁ = to recover, a common news word (הַשּׁוּק הִתְאוֹשֵׁשׁ = the market recovered).

s.line: greatly enjoying the walk through the soft, fresh grass;
s.note: נֶהֱנָה מִ־ = to enjoy, and it takes מִ, "from": נֶהֱנֵיתִי מֵהַסֶּרֶט = I enjoyed the film. תֵּהָנֶה! = enjoy!

s.line: and it was not long before they reached the road of yellow brick and turned again toward the Emerald City where the Great Oz dwelt.
The road was smooth and well paved, now, and the country about was beautiful,
s.note: סָלוּל = paved, a pa'ul (passive) participle of סָלַל (to pave). A מַסְלוּל, from the same root, is a route or track. דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine, so הָיְתָה and חֲלָקָה.

s.line: so that the travelers rejoiced in leaving the forest far behind, and with it the many dangers they had met in its gloomy shades.
s.note: הִשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something behind; נִשְׁאַר (nif'al) = to stay, to remain. הִשְׁאַרְתִּי אֶת הַטֵּלֵפוֹן בַּבַּיִת = I left my phone at home. A מְטַיֵּל is a hiker or a traveler; טִיּוּל = a trip.

s.line: Once more they could see fences built beside the road;

w: שֶׁכַּנִּרְאֶה|in which apparently|~lit. as is seen
s.line: but these were painted green, and when they came to a small house, in which a farmer evidently lived, that also was painted green.
s.note: כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, "as it seems", built from נִרְאֶה. צָבוּעַ (painted) is a pa'ul participle of צָבַע (to paint); צֶבַע = color, paint. A fresh sign in Israel reads זָהִירוּת, צֶבַע טָרִי (careful, wet paint).

w: עַל פְּנֵי|by|~lit. on the face of
s.line: They passed by several of these houses during the afternoon,
s.note: עָבַר עַל פְּנֵי = passed by (without stopping). אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם = afternoon, often shortened in writing to אחה"צ.

s.line: and sometimes people came to the doors and looked at them as if they would like to ask questions;
but no one came near them nor spoke to them because of the great Lion, of which they were very much afraid.
s.note: שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ = "of whom": Hebrew keeps the preposition of פָּחַד מִ־ and attaches it to a pronoun after שֶׁ. Literally "that from him they were afraid". The same pattern gave שֶׁבָּהּ ("that in it") in the paragraph above.

s.line: The people were all dressed in clothing of a lovely emerald-green color and wore peaked hats like those of the Munchkins.
s.note: Hebrew has a different "wear" verb for each part of the body: לָבַשׁ clothes, חָבַשׁ a hat, נָעַל shoes. מְחֻדָּד (sharpened, pointed) is a pu'al participle; חַד = sharp.

s.line: “This must be the Land of Oz,” said Dorothy, “and we are surely getting near the Emerald City.”
s.note: בֶּטַח and בְּוַדַּאי both mean "surely, probably". בֶּטַח is the everyday one, and on its own it means "sure!": – תָּבוֹא? – בֶּטַח!. בְּוַדַּאי is a little more careful.

s.line: “Yes,” answered the Scarecrow.
“Everything is green here, while in the country of the Munchkins blue was the favorite color.
s.note: וְאִלּוּ = whereas, while (for a contrast). Don't confuse it with אִלּוּ = "if only, if" for something unreal. אָהוּב = loved, favorite, a pa'ul participle of אָהַב; הַשִּׁיר הָאָהוּב עָלַי = my favorite song.

s.line: But the people do not seem to be as friendly as the Munchkins,
and I’m afraid we shall be unable to find a place to pass the night.”
s.note: חוֹשֵׁשׁ שֶׁ = "I'm afraid that, I worry that", a bit more careful than פּוֹחֵד. בִּלָּה = to spend (time); on its own it means to go out and have fun: בִּלִּינוּ יָפֶה = we had a great time.

w: הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה|I would like|~conditional: I would want (fem.)
s.line: “I should like something to eat besides fruit,” said the girl, “and I’m sure Toto is nearly starved.
s.note: הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה (past of הָיָה + participle) is the polite "I would like". מֵת מֵרָעָב = "dying of hunger", the everyday exaggeration for "I'm starving"; also מֵת מֵעֲיֵפוּת (dead tired).

s.line: Let us stop at the next house and talk to the people.”
s.note: בּוֹאוּ + future "we" form = "let's": בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ (let's go). To one person you say בּוֹא or בּוֹאִי: בּוֹאִי נִרְאֶה (let's see).

s.line: So, when they came to a good-sized farmhouse, Dorothy walked boldly up to the door and knocked.
s.note: לְמַדַּי = fairly, quite, while מִדַּי = too: גָּדוֹל לְמַדַּי (fairly big) but גָּדוֹל מִדַּי (too big). נִגַּשׁ = to approach; it is nif'al with an active meaning. נִגַּשׁ לַבְּחִינָה = to sit an exam.

s.line: A woman opened it just far enough to look out, and said,
s.note: הֵצִיץ (hif'il) = to peek, to take a quick look. הַחוּצָה = outward, "to the outside": the ending ָה shows direction, as in הַבַּיְתָה (homeward).

s.line: “What do you want, child, and why is that great Lion with you?”
“We wish to pass the night with you, if you will allow us,” answered Dorothy;
s.note: לָלוּן = to stay overnight, from the same root as מָלוֹן (hotel) and לִינָה (lodging). אֶצְלֵךְ = "at your place" (said to a woman); אֶצְלִי = at my place.

w: בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן|for the world|~idiom: in no way
s.line: “and the Lion is my friend and comrade, and would not hurt you for the world.”
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hurt, to hit, to offend (always with בְּ). נִפְגַּעְתִּי = I was hurt or offended, and in the news a פִּגּוּעַ is an attack. בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן with לֹא = "in no way, under no circumstances".

s.line: “Is he tame?” asked the woman, opening the door a little wider.
s.note: מְאֻלָּף = trained, tame, the pu'al participle of אִלֵּף (pi'el), to train an animal. A yes/no question in Hebrew is just a statement said with a rising voice: הוּא מְאֻלָּף?

s.line: “Oh, yes,” said the girl, “and he is a great coward, too.
He will be more afraid of you than you are of him.”
s.note: "To be afraid" is both פָּחַד (pa'al) and פִּחֵד (pi'el), with the same meaning and both with מִ־. In the present the pi'el מְפַחֵד is what you'll hear: אֲנִי מְפַחֵד מִכְּלָבִים. יוֹתֵר … מִמָּה שֶׁ… = more … than.

s.line: “Well,” said the woman, after thinking it over and taking another peep at the Lion,
“if that is the case you may come in, and I will give you some supper and a place to sleep.”
s.note: אִם כָּךְ = if so, in that case (also אִם כֵּן). לְהִכָּנֵס = to come in, nif'al with an active meaning; the dagesh in כּ is typical of the nif'al infinitive. A sign on a door: אֵין כְּנִיסָה = no entry.

s.line: So they all entered the house, where there were, besides the woman, two children and a man.
The man had hurt his leg, and was lying on the couch in a corner.
s.note: נִפְצַע = was injured, the nif'al (passive) of פָּצַע (to wound). You hear it in almost every news report: שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים נִפְצְעוּ קַל (two people were lightly injured). Hebrew says "was injured in the leg", בָּרֶגֶל, not "hurt his leg".

s.line: They seemed greatly surprised to see so strange a company,
s.note: מֻפְתָּע = surprised, the hof'al participle, the passive of הִפְתִּיעַ (hif'il) = to surprise someone. הַפְתָּעָה = a surprise; מְסִבַּת הַפְתָּעָה = a surprise party.

s.line: and while the woman was busy laying the table the man asked:
s.note: עָרַךְ = to arrange: עָרַךְ שֻׁלְחָן (set the table), עָרַךְ מְסִבָּה (threw a party), and עָרַךְ a text = to edit it; עוֹרֵךְ = an editor.

s.line: “Where are you all going?”
s.note: לְאָן = where to; אֵיפֹה = where (at), מֵאַיִן or מֵאֵיפֹה = where from. With a verb of motion Hebrew always says לְאָן.

s.line: “To the Emerald City,” said Dorothy, “to see the Great Oz.”
“Oh, indeed!” exclaimed the man.
“Are you sure that Oz will see you?”
s.note: הִסְכִּים (hif'il) = to agree, often + infinitive: הוּא הִסְכִּים לַעֲזֹר (he agreed to help). הֶסְכֵּם = an agreement, a treaty, a word you'll meet in the news; מַסְכִּים! = "I agree!".

s.line: “Why not?” she replied.
“Why, it is said that he never lets anyone come into his presence.
s.note: נָתַן לְ־ + infinitive = to let someone do something: תֵּן לִי לַעֲבֹר = let me pass. הֲרֵי = "after all, you know", used when the speaker thinks the listener should already know: הֲרֵי אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ!

s.line: I have been to the Emerald City many times, and it is a beautiful and wonderful place;
but I have never been permitted to see the Great Oz, nor do I know of any living person who has seen him.”
s.note: מַכִּיר = to know a person or a place; יוֹדֵעַ = to know a fact. אֲנִי מַכִּיר אוֹתוֹ (I know him) but אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהוּא כָּאן (I know that he's here). הִרְשׁוּ לִי, "they allowed me", with no subject, stands for the English passive "I was permitted".

s.line: “Does he never go out?” asked the Scarecrow.
“Never.
He sits day after day in the great Throne Room of his Palace,
s.note: כֵּס = throne, a literary word; the ordinary chair is כִּסֵּא. שֶׁבָּאַרְמוֹן = "that is in the palace": שֶׁ + a preposition is a short way to say where something is, as in הַבַּיִת שֶׁבַּפִּנָּה (the house on the corner).

w: פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים|face to face|~set phrase
s.line: and even those who wait upon him do not see him face to face.”
s.note: שֵׁרֵת (pi'el) = to serve; שֵׁרוּת = service, and שֵׁרוּת צְבָאִי = military service. שֵׁרוּתִים is also the word for restrooms.

s.line: “What is he like?” asked the girl.
“That is hard to tell,” said the man thoughtfully.
s.note: לְהַגִּיד = to say, to tell. It is the hif'il of נ־ג־ד, and it serves as the infinitive and future of אָמַר in speech: מָה הוּא יַגִּיד? = what will he say? You'll also hear לוֹמַר, the infinitive of אָמַר itself.

s.line: “You see, Oz is a Great Wizard, and can take on any form he wishes.
s.note: לָבַשׁ צוּרָה = "to put on a form", to take a shape, a set phrase לָבַשׁ has besides "to wear". In אוֹז הוּא קוֹסֵם the word הוּא works as "is", linking the subject to a noun.

w: יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים|some say|~set phrase: there are (those) saying
s.line: So that some say he looks like a bird; and some say he looks like an elephant; and some say he looks like a cat.
s.note: יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים = "some say", literally "there are (people) saying". The same pattern: יֵשׁ חוֹשְׁבִים = some think. It sounds slightly bookish but is common in journalism.

w: שֶׁמּוֹצֵאת חֵן בְּעֵינָיו|that pleases him|~idiom: finds favor in his eyes
s.line: To others he appears as a beautiful fairy, or a brownie, or in any other form that pleases him.
s.note: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי = to please, "to find favor in the eyes of": the thing liked is the subject. הַסֶּרֶט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי = I liked the film; here מוֹצֵאת is feminine to agree with צוּרָה. הוֹפִיעַ = to appear, and also to perform: הוֹפָעָה = a concert, a show.

s.line: But who the real Oz is, when he is in his own form, no living person can tell.”
“That is very strange,” said Dorothy, “but we must try, in some way, to see him, or we shall have made our journey for nothing.”
s.note: חַיָּב = must, stronger than צָרִיךְ (should, need to). אֵיכְשֶׁהוּ = somehow; the ending שֶׁהוּ makes "some-" words: מַשֶּׁהוּ (something), מִישֶׁהוּ (someone), אֵיפֹשֶׁהוּ (somewhere).

s.line: “Why do you wish to see the terrible Oz?” asked the man.
“I want him to give me some brains,” said the Scarecrow eagerly.
s.note: "I want him to give" is אֲנִי רוֹצֶה שֶׁהוּא יִתֵּן, "I want that he will give". Hebrew has no "want someone to do"; it uses שֶׁ + future: אֲנִי רוֹצָה שֶׁתָּבוֹא = I want you to come.

s.line: “Oh, Oz could do that easily enough,” declared the man.
s.note: הִכְרִיז (hif'il) = to declare, to announce; הַכְרָזָה = an announcement, a news word (הַכְרָזַת הָעַצְמָאוּת, the Declaration of Independence). A כְּרָזָה is a poster.

w: יֵשׁ לוֹ|he has|~lit. there is to him
s.line: “He has more brains than he needs.”
“And I want him to give me a heart,” said the Tin Woodman.
“That will not trouble him,” continued the man, “for Oz has a large collection of hearts, of all sizes and shapes.”
s.note: הִטְרִיד (hif'il) = to bother, to worry: זֶה מַטְרִיד אוֹתִי = that bothers me; הַטְרָדָה = harassment. The plural of לֵב is לְבָבוֹת, and of גֹּדֶל (size) it is גְּדָלִים.

s.line: “And I want him to give me courage,” said the Cowardly Lion.

w: בְּצַלַּחַת זָהָב|with a golden plate|~lit. plate of gold
s.line: “Oz keeps a great pot of courage in his Throne Room,” said the man, “which he has covered with a golden plate, to keep it from running over.
s.note: גָּלַשׁ = to overflow, to boil over (הֶחָלָב גָּלַשׁ). It is also to slide, ski, or surf, and to browse the web: גּוֹלֵשׁ = a surfer or a web user. כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = so that.

s.line: He will be glad to give you some.”
“And I want him to send me back to Kansas,” said Dorothy.
s.note: הֶחְזִיר (hif'il) = to bring or send back, to return something: the causative of חָזַר (to come back). הֶחְזַרְתִּי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר = I returned the book.

s.line: “Where is Kansas?” asked the man, with surprise.
“I don’t know,” replied Dorothy sorrowfully, “but it is my home, and I’m sure it’s somewhere.”
s.note: נִמְצָא here is nif'al, "is found, is located": אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק? = where is the bank? The same spelling, with the same vowels, is also the pa'al future "we will find": נִמְצָא דֶּרֶךְ = we'll find a way. Only the context tells them apart.

s.line: “Very likely.
s.note: סָבִיר = likely, and also reasonable: מְחִיר סָבִיר = a reasonable price. סָבִיר לְהַנִּיחַ שֶׁ… = it is reasonable to assume that …

s.line: Well, Oz can do anything; so I suppose he will find Kansas for you.
s.note: אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁ… = I suppose, I assume that …; הַנָּחָה = an assumption. A woman says אֲנִי מַנִּיחָה.

s.line: But first you must get to see him, and that will be a hard task;
s.note: הִצְלִיחַ (hif'il) = to succeed, and + infinitive "to manage to": לֹא הִצְלַחְתִּי לִישֹׁן = I couldn't get to sleep. בְּהַצְלָחָה! = good luck!

w: וּבְדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל|and usually|~set phrase: by the general way
עוֹשֶׂה מָה שֶׁהוּא רוֹצֶה|has his own way|~idiom: does what he wants
s.line: for the Great Wizard does not like to see anyone, and he usually has his own way.
s.note: בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל = usually, one of the most common adverbs in speech. עוֹשֶׂה מָה שֶׁהוּא רוֹצֶה = "does what he wants", gets his own way.

s.line: But what do YOU want?” he continued, speaking to Toto.
s.note: פָּנָה אֶל = to turn to, to address someone. פְּנִיָּה = an inquiry or request, the word on official forms (פְּנִיָּה לַצִּבּוּר, a notice to the public), and also a turn on the road.

w: לְמַרְבֶּה הַפֶּלֶא|strange to say|~idiom: to the greatness of the wonder
s.line: Toto only wagged his tail; for, strange to say, he could not speak.
s.note: כִּשְׁכֵּשׁ בַּזָּנָב: a dog wags "with" its tail, with בְּ. לְמַרְבֶּה הַ… = "to the great …": לְמַרְבֶּה הַפֶּלֶא (amazingly), לְמַרְבֶּה הַמַּזָּל (luckily), לְמַרְבֶּה הַצַּעַר (unfortunately).

s.line: The woman now called to them that supper was ready,
s.note: Reported speech in Hebrew keeps the tense of the original words: she said "supper is ready", so אָמְרָה שֶׁהָאֲרוּחָה מוּכָנָה, with no past-tense "was". מוּכָן = ready, a hof'al participle ("made ready") from the root of הֵכִין (to prepare).

s.line: so they gathered around the table and Dorothy ate some delicious porridge and a dish of scrambled eggs and a plate of nice white bread,
s.note: בֵּיצִים מְקֻשְׁקָשׁוֹת = scrambled eggs, a pu'al participle of קִשְׁקֵשׁ, which also means to scribble and to chatter; קִשְׁקוּשִׁים = nonsense. בֵּיצָה is feminine, so the participle ends in וֹת.

s.line: and enjoyed her meal.
The Lion ate some of the porridge, but did not care for it,
saying it was made from oats and oats were food for horses, not for lions.
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of: עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (made of wood). שִׁבֹּלֶת שׁוּעָל (oats) is literally "fox's ear (of grain)". Again the reported speech stays in the present: הִיא עֲשׂוּיָה, "it is made".

s.line: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman ate nothing at all.
Toto ate a little of everything, and was glad to get a good supper again.
The woman now gave Dorothy a bed to sleep in, and Toto lay down beside her,
s.note: מִטָּה לִישֹׁן בָּהּ, "a bed to sleep in it": Hebrew repeats the preposition with a pronoun where English leaves "in" hanging at the end. לְיָדָהּ = beside her, from יָד (hand).

w: כְּדֵי שֶׁאַף אֶחָד|so that no one
s.line: while the Lion guarded the door of her room so she might not be disturbed.
s.note: שָׁמַר עַל = to guard, to look after: שְׁמֹר עַל עַצְמְךָ = take care of yourself. הִפְרִיעַ לְ־ = to disturb, to bother, with לְ: the hotel-door sign is נָא לֹא לְהַפְרִיעַ.

s.line: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman stood up in a corner and kept quiet all night, although of course they could not sleep.
s.note: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although, the same as לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ; often written אע"פ. כַּמּוּבָן = of course, from מוּבָן = understood (a hof'al participle).

w: בְּרֶגַע שֶׁהַשֶּׁמֶשׁ|as soon as the sun|~lit. at the moment that the sun
יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|started on their way|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: The next morning, as soon as the sun was up, they started on their way,
s.note: זָרַח = (the sun) rose, shone; מִזְרָח (east) and זְרִיחָה (sunrise) are from the same root. שֶׁמֶשׁ is normally feminine, so זָרְחָה. לְמָחֳרָת = the next day; מָחָר = tomorrow.

w: וְתוֹךְ זְמַן קָצָר|and soon|~lit. within a short time
s.line: and soon saw a beautiful green glow in the sky just before them.
“That must be the Emerald City,” said Dorothy.

w: כְּכָל שֶׁהֵם|the further they|~lit. as much as they
s.line: As they walked on, the green glow became brighter and brighter, and it seemed that at last they were nearing the end of their travels.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה = became, the nif'al of עָשָׂה; it can also mean "was done". כְּכָל שֶׁ = "the more …": כְּכָל שֶׁעוֹבֵר הַזְּמַן = as time goes by. הִתְקַדֵּם = to move forward, to make progress; הִתְקַדְּמוּת = progress.

s.line: Yet it was afternoon before they came to the great wall that surrounded the City.
s.note: חוֹמָה = a city wall or rampart (חוֹמוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַיִם); the wall of a room is קִיר. הִקִּיף (hif'il) = to surround; מַקִּיף = comprehensive, as in מִבְחָן מַקִּיף.

s.line: It was high and thick and of a bright green color.
In front of them, and at the end of the road of yellow brick, was a big gate,
all studded with emeralds that glittered so in the sun that even the painted eyes of the Scarecrow were dazzled by their brilliancy.
s.note: מְשֻׁבָּץ = set, studded (with jewels), the pu'al participle of שִׁבֵּץ, which also means to fit someone into a slot or schedule; a מִשְׁבֶּצֶת is a square on a grid. הִסְתַּנְוֵר (hitpa'el) = to be dazzled; סִנְוֵר (pi'el) = to dazzle, to blind with light.

s.line: There was a bell beside the gate, and Dorothy pushed the button and heard a silvery tinkle sound within.
s.note: לָחַץ עַל = to press (a button), with עַל: לְחַץ עַל הַקִּשּׁוּר = click on the link. לַחַץ = pressure or stress, and לָחוּץ = stressed out. צִלְצוּל = a ring; צִלְצֵל = to ring, also to phone someone.

s.line: Then the big gate swung slowly open,

w: וּמָצְאוּ אֶת עַצְמָם|and found themselves|~set phrase
s.line: and they all passed through and found themselves in a high arched room, the walls of which glistened with countless emeralds.
s.note: לְלֹא = without, a slightly more formal בְּלִי: לְלֹא תַּשְׁלוּם = free of charge. מְקֻשָּׁת = arched, curved like a קֶשֶׁת (a bow, an arch, and also a rainbow).

s.line: Before them stood a little man about the same size as the Munchkins.
s.note: בְּעֵרֶךְ = about, approximately: בְּעֵרֶךְ שָׁעָה = about an hour. On its own עֵרֶךְ means "value": עֲרָכִים = values, principles.

w: מִכַּף רֶגֶל וְעַד רֹאשׁ|from head to foot|~idiom: from the sole of the foot to the head
s.line: He was clothed all in green, from his head to his feet, and even his skin was of a greenish tint.
s.note: מִכַּף רֶגֶל וְעַד רֹאשׁ = from head to toe; Hebrew goes the other way, from the foot up. יְרַקְרַק = greenish: repeating the last two root letters softens a color, as in אֲדַמְדַּם (reddish) and כְּחַלְחַל (bluish).

s.line: At his side was a large green box.
When he saw Dorothy and her companions the man asked,
“What do you wish in the Emerald City?”
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ (pi'el) = to ask for, to request, to seek; בַּקָּשָׁה = a request, and בְּבַקָּשָׁה (please) is "with a request". To ask a question is שָׁאַל.

s.line: “We came here to see the Great Oz,” said Dorothy.
s.note: לְכָאן = (to) here, used with verbs of motion; כָּאן = here (at). בּוֹא לְכָאן! = come here! In speech you'll also hear לְפֹה.

s.line: The man was so surprised at this answer that he sat down to think it over.
s.note: הֻפְתַּע = was surprised, the hof'al past; its participle is מֻפְתָּע (surprised). כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = so … that: הָיָה כָּל כָּךְ חַם שֶׁלֹּא יָצָאנוּ = it was so hot that we didn't go out.

s.line: “It has been many years since anyone asked me to see Oz,” he said, shaking his head in perplexity.
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־ = to ask something of someone: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ לַעֲזֹר = I asked him to help. מְבוּכָה = embarrassment or confusion; נָבוֹךְ = embarrassed, at a loss.

s.line: “He is powerful and terrible,
and if you come on an idle or foolish errand to bother the wise reflections of the Great Wizard, he might be angry and destroy you all in an instant.”
s.note: עָלוּל = might, liable to, for a bad outcome: עָלוּל לָרֶדֶת גֶּשֶׁם (it might rain). For a neutral or good outcome you use עָשׂוּי. סְתָמִי = pointless, from סְתָם = "just, for no reason", one of the most frequent words in speech.

s.line: “But it is not a foolish errand, nor an idle one,” replied the Scarecrow;
“it is important.
And we have been told that Oz is a good Wizard.”
s.note: סִפְּרוּ לָנוּ, "they told us" with no subject, is how Hebrew says "we have been told", the same trick as אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ….

s.line: “So he is,” said the green man, “and he rules the Emerald City wisely and well.
s.note: שָׁלַט בְּ־ = to rule, to control, with בְּ: הוּא שׁוֹלֵט בְּאַנְגְּלִית = he has a good command of English. שִׁלְטוֹן = government, regime; a TV remote is a שַׁלָּט.

s.line: But to those who are not honest, or who approach him from curiosity, he is most terrible,
s.note: שֶׁאֵינָם = "who are not", אֵין with a pronoun ending, a more careful way to say שֶׁלֹּא. מִתּוֹךְ = out of (a motive): מִתּוֹךְ סַקְרָנוּת, מִתּוֹךְ פַּחַד. סַקְרָן = curious.

s.line: and few have ever dared ask to see his face.
s.note: אֵי פַּעַם = ever: הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת? = have you ever been to Eilat? With לֹא, "never" is אַף פַּעַם. הֵעֵז (hif'il) = to dare; אַל תָּעֵז! = don't you dare!

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: I am the Guardian of the Gates, and since you demand to see the Great Oz I must take you to his Palace.
s.note: דָּרַשׁ = to demand, stronger than בִּקֵּשׁ; דְּרִישָׁה = a demand, a requirement. Job ads start with דְּרוּשִׁים, "wanted", the pa'ul participle. מִכֵּיוָן שֶׁ = since, because.

s.line: But first you must put on the spectacles.”
s.note: Glasses are "mounted": הִרְכִּיב מִשְׁקָפַיִם = to put on glasses, and הוּא מַרְכִּיב מִשְׁקָפַיִם = he wears glasses. The same verb means to assemble (הִרְכִּיב רָהִיט, to put together furniture) and to give someone a ride on a bike or on your shoulders.

s.line: “Why?” asked Dorothy.
“Because if you did not wear spectacles the brightness and glory of the Emerald City would blind you.
s.note: סִנְוֵר (pi'el) = to dazzle, to blind with light; it has two subjects here, so the verb is plural, יְסַנְוְרוּ. הָדָר = splendor, glory, a literary word; מְהֻדָּר = elegant, fancy.

w: יוֹם וָלַיְלָה|night and day|~set phrase: day and night
s.line: Even those who live in the City must wear spectacles night and day.
s.note: יוֹם וָלַיְלָה = day and night, all the time; Hebrew puts the day first. The וָ with a qamats appears in some fixed pairs like this one.

s.line: They are all locked on, for Oz so ordered it when the City was first built,
s.note: נָעוּל = locked, a pa'ul participle of נָעַל, which means both "to lock" and "to put on shoes" (נַעַל = a shoe). נִבְנְתָה = was built, the nif'al (passive) of בָּנָה. צִוָּה (pi'el) = to command; מִצְוָה comes from the same root.

s.line: and I have the only key that will unlock them.”
s.note: מַפְתֵּחַ (key) is built from the root of פָּתַח (to open), in the מַ…ֵ… pattern of tools. אֶצְלִי = with me, in my keeping: הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת אֶצְלִי = I've got the keys.

s.line: He opened the big box, and Dorothy saw that it was filled with spectacles of every size and shape.
All of them had green glasses in them.
s.note: עֲדָשָׁה = a lens, and also a lentil: מְרַק עֲדָשִׁים = lentil soup, עֲדָשׁוֹת מַגָּע = contact lenses.

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: The Guardian of the Gates found a pair that would just fit Dorothy and put them over her eyes.
s.note: הִתְאִים לְ־ = to fit, to suit: זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי = that doesn't suit me / doesn't work for me. מַתְאִים = suitable. זוּג (a pair, also a couple) is masculine, so אוֹתוֹ.

s.line: There were two golden bands fastened to them that passed around the back of her head,
s.note: מְחֻבָּר = attached, connected, the pu'al participle of חִבֵּר (to join; in math, to add): אַתָּה מְחֻבָּר? = are you online? עֹרֶף = the back of the neck; in the news הָעֹרֶף is the home front, the civilians behind the front line.

w: זוֹ לְזוֹ|together|~lit. this one to this one (fem.)
שֶׁשּׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|that the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: where they were locked together by a little key that was at the end of a chain the Guardian of the Gates wore around his neck.
s.note: Another "wear" verb: עָנַד is for jewelry, chains and watches (עָנַד שָׁעוֹן). So: לָבַשׁ clothes, חָבַשׁ a hat, נָעַל shoes, הִרְכִּיב glasses, עָנַד jewelry. תָּלוּי = hanging; זֶה תָּלוּי = it depends.

w: הָיְתָה יְכוֹלָה|could have|~conditional: would be able (fem.)
s.line: When they were on, Dorothy could not take them off had she wished,
s.note: הוֹרִיד (hif'il of יָרַד, "to make go down") = to take off (clothes, glasses), to lower, and to download: הוֹרַדְתִּי אֶת הָאַפְּלִיקַצְיָה. הָיְתָה רוֹצָה: הָיָה + participle again gives "would (have)".

s.line: but of course she did not wish to be blinded by the glare of the Emerald City, so she said nothing.
s.note: לֹא אָמְרָה דָּבָר = said nothing; after לֹא the word דָּבָר means "anything", a little more careful than כְּלוּם. הִסְתַּנְוֵר (hitpa'el) is the "be dazzled" partner of סִנְוֵר.

s.line: Then the green man fitted spectacles for the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and the Lion, and even on little Toto;
s.note: Here הִתְאִים takes an object: "to fit something to someone", to adjust. After אַחַר כָּךְ or אָז at the start of a sentence, Hebrew narrative often puts the verb before the subject: הִתְאִים הָאִישׁ.

s.line: and all were locked fast with the key.

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: Then the Guardian of the Gates put on his own glasses and told them he was ready to show them to the Palace.
Taking a big golden key from a peg on the wall, he opened another gate,
s.note: נוֹסָף = another, additional; בְּנוֹסָף = in addition, and עוֹד is the everyday "another": עוֹד שַׁעַר. A וָו is a hook or peg; it is also the name of the letter ו.

s.line: and they all followed him through the portal into the streets of the Emerald City.
s.note: הָלַךְ אַחֲרֵי = to follow, "to go after". To follow someone online is עָקַב אַחֲרֵי, and followers are עוֹקְבִים.
